title: What's the deal with headstones?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of headstones and grave markers, from prehistoric burial rites and Neanderthal burials through Celtic and Roman stones, cairns, churchyards, and the Rural Cemetery Movement. They cover symbolism on gravestones (Celtic cross, Puritan death's head, Victorian symbols), colonial-era epitaphs, and the history of Civil War and national cemetery military markers, including the 1873 marble standard. The episode also covers unmarked graves (potter's fields, executed criminals, famous people such as Mozart, Jim Morrison, John Wayne, Bobby Driscoll), a few epitaph examples, and a listener mail item about mismatched podcast voices and faces.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about naps and the episode's sources, then introduce the topic of headstones and grave markers and note it pairs with the coffins episode.

segments.title: Prehistoric and Neanderthal burials
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early evidence of funeral rites among primates and Neanderthals, the possible role of disgust and smell in burial, and an early anatomically modern human child burial.

segments.title: Early stones, Celtic and Roman markers, and cairns
segments.summary: Early headstones in Roman and Celtic times were detailed, showing battles and professions. Stelae were upright memorial stones, the term headstone may come from Jewish grave-marking custom, and cairns protected bodies from scavengers.

segments.title: Churchyards and the Rural Cemetery Movement
segments.summary: Pre-nineteenth-century burials were near family plots and later moved to churchyards. The Rural Cemetery Movement brought landscaped, park-like cemeteries to city outskirts, where families sometimes picnicked.

segments.title: Celtic cross, memento mori, and colonial gravestones
segments.summary: The Celtic cross combined a sun cross with a Christian cross. Irish epitaphs were witty, and colonial American stones used limestone, marble, and later igneous rock. Puritans used death's head carvings to remind viewers of hell.

segments.title: Victorian gravestone symbolism
segments.summary: Victorian headstones used hopeful symbols such as wheat, gates, butterflies, broken columns, broken flowers, buds, hourglasses, lamps, and clasped hands. Iron mort safes were used to protect bodies from grave robbers for anatomists.

segments.title: Modern headstones and famous epitaphs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the modern headstone industry and go through several humorous or notable epitaphs, referencing the show's slideshow of twenty-one remarkable epitaphs, including Charles Kowski and Robert Clay Allison.

segments.title: Y2K and pre-carved gravestone dates
segments.summary: Some people pre-purchased headstones dated 19 with the second half blank, so the Y2K problem meant many had to be re-etched in the 2000s.

segments.title: Military headstones and the Civil War
segments.summary: Early military graves were marked with wooden boards and sometimes mass graves. After the Civil War, cost and decay of wooden markers led to a debate between marble and galvanized iron, and marble was chosen in 1873. Standard dimensions were 39 by 12 by 4 inches, with 12 inches above ground. Government headstones are also called Obama stones in the transcript's joke.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener writes about mismatched voices and faces from the hosts, and the hosts give their social media and website information before signing off.
